entry.evidence: we decided to further investigate the crystal chemical evolution and thermoelastic properties of this phase

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML text (jats_text), checked against the published PDF

steps.action: Take from other groups' phase-equilibrium experiments the idea that high-pressure Ca-rich alkaline carbonates, burbankite among them, may fractionate elements from upper-mantle carbonatitic melts.
steps.quote: their high-pressure phases may fractionate elements from a carbonatitic melt crystallizing in upper-mantle conditions

steps.action: Rely on the authors' earlier synthesis of Na3Ca2La(CO3)5 at 5 GPa and 1073 K, which showed that LREE3+ can be incorporated into a burbankite-like structure.
steps.quote: the successful synthesis of Na 3 Ca 2 La(CO 3 ) 5 at 5 GPa and 1073 K (Merlini et al., 2020)

steps.action: Pose the aim of determining the crystal-chemical evolution and thermoelastic properties of synthetic La-burbankite at high pressure and high temperature.
steps.quote: we decided to further investigate the crystal chemical evolution and thermoelastic properties of this phase

steps.action: Synthesize single crystals (up to 500 µm) in a multi-anvil press from stoichiometric carbonate powders in a welded Pt capsule at 5 GPa and 1073 K for 24 h; the run yields burbankite plus a Ca-rich La oxide.
steps.quote: Samples were synthesized at 5 GPa and 1073 K

steps.action: Design the in situ high-pressure single-crystal XRD test at Elettra Xpress: BX90 diamond-anvil cell, 4:1 methanol:ethanol medium (hydrostatic by citation), ruby pressure standard, pressures up to 7.07 GPa.
steps.quote: A synthetic single crystal of burbankite was loaded in a BX90-type diamond-anvil cell

steps.action: Improve the beamline data-collection protocol (absorption-based automatic alignment, slower step scans, synchronized fast shutter), which lowers Rint of integrated intensities to 2 % and makes structure refinement in the DAC possible.
steps.quote: improvement in data collection protocols has been specifically designed

steps.action: Design the in situ high-temperature single-crystal XRD test at Elettra XRD1: crystal in a quartz-glass capillary with a quartz standard crystal, heated by hot-air blower in 30 K steps from 298 K up to about 746 K.
steps.quote: a hot air gas blower was used to increase the T every 30 K

steps.action: Measure 20 EMPA points on the synthetic batch and derive an average empirical formula that shows A-site vacancies.
steps.quote: Based on the empirical formula calculated on the EMPA data, some vacancies have been evidenced.

steps.action: Solve and refine the ambient structure in P63mc with Jana2006 (consistent with earlier studies), giving cell constants, atomic coordinates and site occupancies (Na,Ca on A; Ca,La on B).
steps.quote: The site occupancy refinement confirms the presence of Na and Ca in the A site, and of Ca and La in the B site.

steps.action: Record unit-cell parameters at 11 pressures (Table 4, Figure 3); the volume decreases smoothly with no phase transition up to about 7 GPa.
steps.quote: No phase transition or change in the deformation mechanisms occurs within the P range investigated.

steps.action: Fit the weighted P–V data with a second-order Birch–Murnaghan EoS in EoSFit7c to obtain V0 and KT0 with K' fixed at 4, and derive axial compressibilities showing the a axis is stiffer than c (Fig. S2).
steps.quote: giving V 0 = 593.22(3) Å 3 , K T 0 = 69.8(4) GPa and K ′ = 4 fixed

steps.action: Check the second-order truncation (K' = 4) with an Fe–fe plot that is fitted by a horizontal line (supplement Fig. S1).
steps.quote: plot (Fe–fe plot, Fig. S1 in the Supplement) of the data can be fitted by a horizontal line

steps.action: Record unit-cell parameters at ambient pressure and increasing temperature (Table 5, Figure 4); the volume rises continuously with no phase transition.
steps.quote: V increases continuously without evidence of phase transition up to the maximum T reached in this study

steps.action: Fit the V–T data with a Berman-type thermal EoS in EoSFit7c to obtain α0, α1 and V0, and derive anisotropic axial thermal expansion (Fig. S3).
steps.quote: [...] data were fitted using EosFit7c (Angel et al., 2014) using a Berman-type equation of state (EoS)

steps.action: Fit BM2 EoS to the polyhedral volumes from refinements at pressure (AO8 KT0 = 54(2) GPa, BO10 KT0 = 72(3) GPa) and report similar thermal expansion of both polyhedra.
steps.quote: we obtain K T 0 = 54(2) GPa for the 8-fold coordinated polyhedra

steps.action: Set the synthesis result against published experimental phase diagrams to argue that La-burbankite is stable at 5 GPa and is a candidate LREE fractionating phase.
steps.quote: Our experiments indicate that La burbankite is still stable at 5 GPa

steps.action: Calculate the density of burbankite at 5.5–6 GPa and 1173–1273 K (about 3.2 g cm-3) using the Holland and Powell (2011) equation of state for solids with the new thermoelastic parameters.
steps.quote: Density has been calculated using the equation of state for solids from Holland and Powell (2011).

steps.action: Compare the computed burbankite density with published carbonatitic magma densities at the same conditions (2.058–3.1 g cm-3, Jones et al. 2013).
steps.quote: [...] the density of carbonatitic magmas in the same P and T conditions

steps.action: Keep the suggestion that burbankite could fractionate from carbonatitic magma as an upper-mantle LREE3+ reservoir, so La is not always incompatible.
steps.quote: the burbankite might fractionate from the magma and play a key role as an upper-mantle reservoir

steps.action: Compare the polyhedral bulk moduli with the inverse-relationship expectation of Hazen and Finger (1982); the larger BO10 polyhedron is stiffer, opposite to that expectation.
steps.quote: the two independent A and B polyhedra might not obey the inverse relationship

steps.action: Refine the scope of the inverse relationship: burbankite as another exception, tentatively attributed to two cation-polyhedron types besides the rigid carbonate unit.
steps.quote: Burbankite could therefore be another example where the inverse relationship is not rigorously true

tree.answer: Known phase (La-burbankite synthesized at 5 GPa); thermoelastic behaviour unknown
Cell volumes observed directly by in situ XRD; moduli and expansivities inferred by EoS fits
Estimate bulk modulus, thermal expansion and structural evolution
No rivals for the EoS; only the inverse-relationship expectation for the polyhedra
Conditions set in the laboratory (multi-anvil, DAC, gas blower)
Only an Fe–fe truncation check; single crystal per experiment, no replicate run
EoS and thermal-expansion parameters kept with uncertainties; fractionation suggested

end.claim: Na3Ca2La(CO3)5 burbankite follows a second-order Birch–Murnaghan EoS with V0 = 593.22(3) Å3 and KT0 = 69.8(4) GPa to 7 GPa, and a Berman-type thermal EoS with stated α0 and α1, with no phase transition in either range.

decisive_move.sentence: Fitting the in situ synchrotron P–V data with the BM2 EoS (and the V–T data with a Berman EoS) produces the thermoelastic parameters on which the density and fractionation argument rests.

gates.evidence: The fractionation idea (§1 ¶5) motivated choosing this phase, but the HP/HT measurements are characterization runs, not designed around a stated hypothesis. The EoS estimate faces no test it could fail beyond the Fe–fe truncation check (§3 ¶3). The density comparison with magma densities (§4 ¶2) could in principle have gone the other way. Nothing is stated as fixed in advance.

imports.item: Birch–Murnaghan finite-strain equation of state (Birch 1947, Phys. Rev.)
synchrotron radiation single-crystal X-ray diffraction (Elettra Xpress and XRD1 beamlines)
BX90 diamond-anvil cell with ruby fluorescence pressure standard
hydrostatic limits of pressure-transmitting media (Klotz et al. 2009, J. Phys. D)
Jana2006 structure refinement, CrysAlis Pro data reduction and VESTA visualization software

novelty_claims.quote: can provide us with a first tool to determine the density of La burbankite in upper-mantle conditions

limits:
Composition is none_fits: the walk is a laboratory characterization of a previously synthesized phase (set conditions, parameter estimation, no stated rivals and no crucial test), so none of the listed compositions applies.

Internal inconsistencies, not explained:
- The abstract gives α0 = 6.0(2)e-5, α1 = 5.7(7)e-8 and V0 = 591.95(8), while §3 ¶4 gives 6.4(1)e-5, 3.3(5)e-8 and 591.86(4). The text does not say which fit is final or why they differ (inference: a refit during revision).
- The HT range is stated as 298–746 K, but Table 5 and Figure 4 end at 628 K.
- §4 ¶2 prints 1731–1273 K where the abstract has 1173–1273 K.
- §3 ¶5 says the polyhedra show an inverse behaviour (Hazen and Finger 1982), while §4 ¶3 says they might not obey the inverse relationship.
- The three ambient-volume values (591.97, 593.22, 591.86 Å3) are not compared.

Gaps in reported checks:
- Each experiment uses one crystal; no replicate run or second crystal is reported.
- The quartz standard and the ruby calibration results are not reported.
- Hydrostaticity rests on a citation.
- EMPA totals of about 59 wt% reflect unanalysed CO2; this is inference.
- The density estimate (about 3.2 g cm-3) has no uncertainty and is extrapolated well beyond the measured T range. Its margin over the upper magma density (3.1) is small.

Sub-claim statuses:
- Burbankite as an upper-mantle LREE reservoir and La not always incompatible: best_explanation at most. It is a suggestion from one density comparison, untested.
- Burbankite as an exception to the inverse relationship: best_explanation, with a tentative cause.
- La-burbankite stable at 5 GPa: rests on the synthesis, which repeats the authors' earlier result.

Missing documents: the supplement (Figs. S1–S3, Tables S1–S4) was not supplied, so the steps citing it are coded from main-text statements. The paper names two referees and an editor, but no review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded.

disagreements.target: Inverse relationship between polyhedral size and compressibility (Hazen and Finger, 1982)
disagreements.support: Polyhedral BM2 fits give a larger bulk modulus for the larger BO10 polyhedron (72 GPa) than for AO8 (54 GPa), opposite to the expectation.
disagreements.quote: In this study we report a bulk modulus (K T 0 = 72 GPa) for the 10-fold coordination polyhedra greater than the bulk modulus

disagreements.target: Incompatible behaviour of La, as in silicate systems
disagreements.support: Burbankite's computed density exceeds that of carbonatitic magmas at 5.5–6 GPa, so it could fractionate and retain La.
disagreements.quote: La does not always have an incompatible behaviour as is the case for silicate systems

alternatives_considered.chosen: second-order Birch–Murnaghan EoS with K' fixed at 4
alternatives_considered.alternatives: higher-order EoS (implied by the Fe–fe test, not named)
alternatives_considered.reason: the Fe–fe plot of the data can be fitted by a horizontal line
